Love for God expressed through obedience (verses 1–7)

Moses joined two duties that must always belong together: love the Lord and keep his commands.

Love leads to obedience.

Only obedience flowing from love is truly acceptable to God (1 John 5:3).

Moses recalled the great and fearful works of God that Israel had witnessed.

What we see with our own eyes, especially during our earliest years, should continue to influence us and improve our lives long afterward.

Blessings and warnings for Israel (verses 8–17)

Moses placed life and death, blessings and curses, before the people.

Their future depended on how they responded to the Lord's commands.

Sin tends to shorten human lives and to shorten a nation's prosperity.

If the people loved and served God, the Lord promised them abundant good gifts.

Godliness includes promises for the present life.

But the favor of God brings more true joy to the heart than an increase in grain, wine or oil.

Turning from the Lord to idols would lead to Israel's ruin.

Take care not to let your heart deceive you.

Everyone who abandons God to set the heart on a created thing will eventually discover that it was a terrible mistake.

Such people have contributed to their own destruction.

Their guilt is greater because they neglected the warnings they had been given.

Keeping God's word in heart, sight and speech (verses 18–25)

Henry identifies three rules for living under God's word.

First, fill the heart with God's word.

Good conduct cannot continue without good thoughts, desires and convictions within us.

Second, keep the eyes fixed on God's word.

Treat it as the guide for your path and the rule governing your work (Psalm 119:30).

Third, employ the tongue in speaking about God's word.

Thoughtful teaching and conversation help God's truth remain alive among the people.

Nothing contributes more to a nation's prosperity and the preservation of true faith than the faithful religious education of children.

The blessing and curse announced (verses 26–32)

Moses summarized every reason to obey in two expressions: the blessing and the curse.

The people had to choose which they would receive.

He appointed a public and solemn proclamation of both, on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.

We have broken God's law and fallen under its curse.

We cannot remedy that condition through our own power.

But in mercy, the gospel places a blessing and a curse before us again.

There is blessing for those who answer its call to repent, believe in Christ and receive new hearts and transformed lives through him.

There is terrible judgment for those who neglect such great salvation.

Let us welcome this good news with thanksgiving and joy.

Do not harden your hearts.

Hear God's voice while it is still called today, while he invites us to approach his throne of mercy.

Be diligent to make your calling and election sure.

Let us be diligent to make our calling and election sure.

Israel must reject pagan worship practices (verses 1–4)

Moses began explaining the laws Israel had to observe in Canaan with instructions about worshiping God.

The Israelites were not to introduce the customs and rituals of idolaters into their worship of the true God, even under the pretext of improving it.

We cannot serve both God and wealth.

We cannot worship both the living God and idols.

Nor can we claim to trust in Jesus Christ while also resting our hope on superstition or self-righteousness.

The place chosen by God and the worship he accepts (verses 5–32)

The command to bring sacrifices to the entrance of the tabernacle was now explained in view of Israel's settlement in Canaan.

Moral duties of worship were different.

People could pray and worship God wherever they lived, as they later did in synagogues.

The place God would choose for sacrifices was described as the place where he would put his name.

It would be his dwelling, where he, the King of Israel, could be approached reverently by his people.

Under the gospel there is no temple or altar that makes offerings acceptable except Christ himself.

The prophets foretold that spiritual incense would be offered to God everywhere (Malachi 1:11).

Jesus declared that true worshipers are accepted when they worship God in spirit and truth, not because they come to one mountain or to Jerusalem (John 4:21).

Even an Israelite who could not bring a sacrifice to the altar could honor God, maintain fellowship with him and receive his mercy.

The work of God should be done with holy joy and cheerfulness.

Children and servants were to rejoice before him as well.

Worship should be a pleasure and delight, not a dreary task.

People should be kind to ministers who instruct them faithfully and set them a good example.

We will continue needing their ministry until we reach a world where religious ordinances are no longer necessary.

Whether we eat or drink, or do anything else, everything should be done for God's glory.

Whatever we do should be done in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, thanking the Father through him.

Israel was not even to investigate the methods used in idol worship.

What spiritual advantage could come from exploring such depths of Satan?

We will find increasing contentment as we grow in love and good works springing from faith and the indwelling Spirit of Christ.

Resisting false religious teaching (verses 1–5)

Moses had already warned about the danger posed by the Canaanites. Now he warned against idolatry arising within Israel itself.

We must become familiar with the truths and commands of Scripture, because temptation often comes disguised as something good and error may appear to be truth.

Only the clear and explicit testimony of God's word can reliably expose such deception.

Sincere love for God is shown by refusing to abandon him and serve false gods, even when the temptation is presented attractively.

Resisting temptation from loved ones (verses 6–11)

Satan often seeks to lead us into evil through people we love.

We are least likely to suspect them of intending harm, are eager to please them and find it natural to follow their example.

The person tempting us might be a brother, child, wife or close friend—someone bound to us by family or affection.

Even so, we must put God and faithfulness to him before our dearest earthly relationships.

We must not break God's law merely to please those we love.

We should refuse the invitation, even if the reason for considering it is curiosity, companionship or a desire to gain the person's affection.

“If sinners entice you, do not consent” (Proverbs 1:10).

Henry also reminds his readers that people must not obstruct God's justice.

The case of an idolatrous Israelite city (verses 12–18)

The law describes an Israelite city turning away from its God to worship idols.

Henry observes that even when ancient Israel was commanded to preserve its faith through force, it was not permitted to compel outsiders into that faith through fire and sword.

He distinguishes those ancient civil judgments from the gospel era.

Under the Christian dispensation, the spiritual judgments at stake are more dreadful than the execution of criminals.

Christians still have every reason to fear God's anger against sin.

We should especially beware the spiritual idolatry of greed and devotion to worldly pleasure.

Parents must not encourage such idolatry by their example or in the way they raise their children.

May the Lord write his law and truth upon our hearts, reign there and pour his love into us!

The enticement here is supposed to come from a brother or child, who are near by nature; from a wife or friend, who are near by choice, and are to us as our souls. Here is the case of a city revolting from the God of Israel, and serving other gods. The crime is supposed to be committed by one of the cities of Israel. Even when they were ordered to preserve their religion by force, yet they were not allowed to bring others to it by fire and sword. Spiritual judgments under the Christian dispensation are more terrible than the execution of criminals; we have not less cause than the Israelites had, to fear the Divine wrath. Let us then fear the spiritual idolatry of covetousness, and the love of worldly pleasure; and be careful not to countenance them in our families, by our example or by the education of our children. May the Lord write his law and truth in our hearts, there set up his throne, and shed abroad his love!

The privileges and holiness of God's people (verses 1–21)

Moses described three privileges God had given Israel to distinguish the people from other nations.

They were honors in themselves and pictures of the spiritual blessings believers receive in Christ.

First, election. “The Lord has chosen you.”

God did not choose Israel because the people had already made themselves superior to other nations.

He chose them through grace so they would become his own.

Believers are chosen in the same way (Ephesians 1:4).

Second, adoption. “You are children of the Lord your God.”

God did not need children, but the people needed a Father.

Every true spiritual Israelite is a child of God and shares in his favor and in the character he forms within his people.

Third, sanctification. “You are a holy people.”

God's people are called to holiness, yet any genuine holiness they possess comes from his grace.

Those whom he chooses as his children, he also forms into a people devoted to good works.

They should avoid whatever could bring disgrace upon their confession of faith in the eyes of those watching for their failures.

Our heavenly Father forbids nothing except for our benefit.

Do not destroy your health, reputation, family happiness or peace of mind.

Above all, do not ruin your soul.

Do not become a slave to bodily appetites or passions, making both yourself and others miserable.

Seek what is best and most useful.

The ceremonial rules regarding unclean animal flesh helped keep Israel separate from idolatrous neighbors.

The gospel makes clear that Christians are no longer bound by those food laws.

But we should ask whether we are truly God's children, separated from worldly ungodliness and dedicated to his glory through Christ's blood.

Does the Holy Spirit work within us?

Lord, teach us through these laws how pure and holy your people ought to live!

Tithes, generosity and care for the poor (verses 22–29)

A second portion of the land's produce was required.

The arrangement opposed human greed, mistrust and selfishness.

It encouraged friendliness, generosity and cheerfulness.

It also established provision for people who were poor.

Israel learned that earthly possessions are enjoyed most comfortably when shared with brothers and sisters in need.

God promised to bless the work of those who served him and did good with what they had.

His blessing is essential to earthly prosperity.

Without it, our efforts can achieve nothing lasting.

Yet that blessing rests upon working hands.

We should not expect God to bless idleness and the love of ease.

It rests also upon giving hands.

People who distribute their possessions generously may find their resources increased.

Free and generous support of religion and other good work is a safe and fruitful way of using wealth.

Chapter 14
Chapter Outline
The Israelites to distinguish themselves from other nations. | (1-21) |
Respecting the application of tithes. | (22-29) |
Verses 1-21
Moses tells the people of Israel how God had given them three distinguishing privileges, which were their honour, and figures of those spiritual blessings in heavenly things, with which God has in Christ blessed us. Here is election; "The Lord hath chosen thee." He did not choose them because they were by their own acts a peculiar people to him above other nations, but he chose them that they might be so by his grace; and thus were believers chosen, [Eph.1.4] Ep 1:4. Here is adoption; "Ye are the children of the Lord your God;" not because God needed children, but because they were orphans, and needed a father. Every spiritual Israelite is indeed a child of God, a partaker of his nature and favour. Here is sanctification; "Thou art a holy people." God's people are required to be holy, and if they are holy, they are indebted to the grace God which makes them so. Those whom God chooses to be his children, he will form to be a holy people, and zealous of good works. They must be careful to avoid every thing which might disgrace their profession, in the sight of those who watch for their halting. Our heavenly Father forbids nothing but for our welfare. Do thyself no harm; do not ruin thy health, thy reputation, thy domestic comforts, thy peace of mind. Especially do not murder thy soul. Do not be the vile slave of thy appetites and passions. Do not render all around thee miserable, and thyself wretched; but aim at that which is most excellent and useful. The laws which regarded many sorts of flesh as unclean, were to keep them from mingling with their idolatrous neighbours. It is plain in the gospel, that these laws are now done away. But let us ask our own hearts, Are we of the children of the Lord our God? Are we separate from the ungodly world, in being set apart to God's glory, the purchase of Christ's blood? Are we subjects of the work of the Holy Ghost? Lord, teach us from these precepts how pure and holy all thy people ought to live!
[Deut.14.22-Deut.14.29]
Verses 22-29
A second portion from the produce of their land was required. The whole appointment evidently was against the covetousness, distrust, and selfishness of the human heart. It promoted friendliness, liberality, and cheerfulness, and raised a fund for the relief of the poor. They were taught that their worldly portion was most comfortably enjoyed, when shared with their brethren who were in want. If we thus serve God, and do good with what we have, it is promised that the Lord our God will bless us in all the works of our land. The blessing of God is all to our outward prosperity; and without that blessing, the work of our hands will bring nothing to pass. The blessing descends upon the working hand. Expect not that God should bless thee in thy idleness and love of ease. And it descends upon the giving hand. He who thus scatters, certainly increases; and to be free and generous in the support of religion, and any good work, is the surest and safest way of thriving.

The year of release and generosity to the poor (verses 1–11)

The year of release pictured the grace of the gospel.

Through it, the Lord proclaims the acceptable year of salvation, in which our debts—our sins—are forgiven.

God's law is spiritual.

It restrains even the thoughts of our hearts.

We are mistaken if we think our thoughts are outside his knowledge or authority.

The law's command to forgive debts exposed the evil in some hearts.

Instead of being generous, certain people refused to lend or give because the year of release was approaching.

They used a law of generosity as an excuse for selfishness.

To avoid committing sin, we must reject sinful thoughts before they produce actions.

It is dreadful to make poor people cry out against us with good reason.

Do not resent helping a neighbor, and do not distrust God's provision.

Give freely and cheerfully, because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).

The release of servants (verses 12–18)

The law concerning Hebrew servants was repeated.

It included a requirement that masters provide some resources when servants were released, so that people who had worked without wages could begin to support themselves.

When members of a household take their duties toward one another seriously, they can expect God to bless their family life.

We should remember that we owe divine justice a debt we cannot pay.

We are like poor, dying slaves.

But the Lord Jesus Christ became poor and shed his blood so that our debt could be paid, our souls ransomed and all our needs supplied.

When the gospel is preached clearly, the Lord's year of release is announced.

It proclaims forgiveness of sin, freedom for the soul and rest in Christ.

As faith in Christ and love for him grow, they overcome selfishness and the world's unkindness.

They remove the excuses that unbelief, mistrust and greed continually invent.

The firstborn animals (verses 19–23)

This law prescribed what Israelites were to do with the firstborn animals of their flocks and herds.

Christians are not bound by that distinction.

We no longer make a difference between the first calf or lamb and the animals that follow.

Instead, we should apply the gospel lesson.

Dedicate yourself—and the first and best of your time and strength—to God.

Use every comfort and possession for his praise and according to his law, remembering that everything we enjoy came from his hand.

The three annual feasts (verses 1–17)

Moses repeated the instructions for the three yearly festivals: Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles.

He also repeated the general requirement that Israel's people gather before God.

Believers must never forget the depth of guilt and suffering from which they have been rescued, or the great price their Redeemer paid.

Remembering that price allows gratitude and joy to live alongside sorrow for sin and patience through the hardships on the road to heaven.

The Israelites were to rejoice in what they received from God and in the worship and offerings they returned to him.

Our duty should be our delight.

Those who lived under the law were commanded to rejoice before God.

How much more should those living under the grace of the gospel rejoice!

Our duty is to rejoice continually and to rejoice in the Lord always.

When we rejoice in him, we should help others rejoice as well, comforting people who grieve and providing for those in need.

Everyone whose joy rests in God can rejoice in hope, because the One who made the promises is faithful.

Just judges and the rejection of idols (verses 18–22)

Moses gave instructions for the proper administration of justice.

Personal favoritism must be set aside.

Everyone should receive what is right, and no one should be wronged.

The people were also warned not to adopt the idolatrous practices of the surrounding nations.

Nothing misrepresents God more seriously—or damages human minds more deeply—than trying to portray the almighty and eternal Spirit, present everywhere, through a physical image and then worshiping that image.

Sadly, even under the gospel, with its better promises, human hearts still tend to create idols in one form or another.

Proper offerings and judgment on idolatry (verses 1–7)

No animal with a defect was to be brought to God as a sacrifice.

This reminds us of Jesus Christ, whose sacrifice was perfect, pure and without blemish.

It also reminds us to give God the best of our abilities, time and possessions.

If we deliberately withhold our best, our claimed obedience becomes hateful to him.

The Mosaic law ordered an Israelite idol worshiper to be put to death by stoning.

Henry treats this ancient, severe judicial sentence as a warning about how seriously God judges idolatry.

He urges people in his own day who have set up idols in their hearts to consider the judgment ancient Israel faced.

This is a description of Israel's historical law and Henry's spiritual application, not an instruction for private punishment today.

Difficult cases and the courts (verses 8–13)

Courts of judgment were to be established in Israel's towns.

The decisions of those courts did not have the direct authority of a divine oracle.

Nevertheless, they were to be made by wise, prudent and experienced judges.

They also benefited from God's promise concerning the administration of justice.

Choosing and instructing a king (verses 14–20)

The Lord himself was Israel's King in a special way.

If the people placed a human king over themselves, that person had to be the one God chose.

Later, when Israel asked for a king, the people approached Samuel, a prophet of the Lord.

Whenever God's choice can be known, it should guide and overrule our own preference.

Moses gave instructions for Israel's future king.

He must avoid everything that would turn him away from God and faithful worship.

Three major obstacles to devotion are wealth, honor and pleasure.

These correspond to the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life.

They are especially dangerous to people who hold positions of authority.

The king was therefore required to study God's law and make it the standard for his rule.

He was to write his own copy of Scripture and read it every day throughout his life.

Merely owning a Bible is not enough.

We must use it, and use it daily for as long as we live.

Christ's disciples never outgrow Scripture.

They will continue needing it until they reach the place where love and knowledge are made perfect.

And the king's copying and reading were worthless if he did not practice what he wrote and read.

Those who fear God and keep his commandments will benefit even in this present life.

No creature which had any blemish was to be offered in sacrifice to God. We are thus called to remember the perfect, pure, and spotless sacrifice of Christ, and reminded to serve God with the best of our abilities, time, and possession, or our pretended obedience will be hateful to him. So great a punishment as death, so remarkable a death as stoning, must be inflicted on the Jewish idolater. Let all who in our day set up idols in their hearts, remember how God punished this crime in Israel.
[Deut.17.8-Deut.17.13]
Verses 8-13
Courts of judgment were to be set up in every city. Though their judgment had not the Divine authority of an oracle, it was the judgment of wise, prudent, experienced men, and had the advantage of a Divine promise.
[Deut.17.14-Deut.17.20]
Verses 14-20
God himself was in a particular manner Israel's King; and if they set another over them, it was necessary that he should choose the person. Accordingly, when the people desired a king, they applied to Samuel, a prophet of the Lord. In all cases, God's choice, if we can but know it, should direct, determine, and overrule ours. Laws are given for the prince that should be elected. He must carefully avoid every thing that would turn him from God and religion. Riches, honours, and pleasures, are three great hinderances of godliness, (the lusts of the flesh, the lusts of the eye, and the pride of life,) especially to those in high stations; against these the king is here warned. The king must carefully study the law of God, and make that his rule; and having a copy of the Scriptures of his own writing, must read therein all the days of his life. It is not enough to have Bibles, but we must use them, use them daily, as long as we live. Christ's scholars never learn above their Bibles, but will have constant occasion for them, till they come to that world where knowledge and love will be made perfect. The king's writing and reading were as nothing, if he did not practise what he wrote and read. And those who fear God and keep his commandments, will fare the better for it even in this world.

Provision for the priests and Levites (verses 1–8)

God took care that the priests would not become entangled in ordinary worldly business or seek to enrich themselves with the world's wealth.

They had more important work to do.

But the Lord also made provision so that they would not lack the ordinary comforts and necessities of life.

The people were responsible for supporting them.

Those who benefit from gathered worship ought to contribute to the adequate support of the ministers who serve and teach them.

Israel must avoid occult practices (verses 9–14)

Israel had received extraordinary blessings from God.

Yet the people remained at risk of turning to false teachers among the nations God had placed under judgment.

Moses therefore repeated the warning not to imitate the abominations of the Canaanites.

Henry explicitly condemns belief in lucky or unlucky days, charms for curing illness, amulets or spells intended to prevent harm, and fortune-telling.

These practices contributed to the judgment that fell upon Canaan.

Henry expresses astonishment that people still claimed occult powers in an age with such broad access to divine truth.

He regards them as impostors who deceive and exploit their followers.

Jesus Christ, the promised great Prophet (verses 15–22)

God promised to raise up a Prophet greater than all the prophets who came before.

Through him, God would reveal himself and his will to humanity more fully and clearly than ever before.

Henry identifies this Prophet as Jesus Christ.

He is the Light of the world (John 8:12).

He is the Word through whom God speaks to us (John 1:1; Hebrews 1:2).

Through his birth, he belonged to Israel.

In his resurrection, he rose in Jerusalem, and his teaching went out from there to the whole world.

God raised up his Son Jesus to bless us.

Christ is like Moses, but infinitely greater.

The promised Prophet has already come.

We are not to look for another.

His revelation of God is meant not to crush us with terror but to give us encouragement.

He speaks with both a father's tenderness and God's own authority.

Anyone who refuses to listen to Christ does so at great risk.

The One appointed as Prophet will also be Judge (John 12:48).

Those who reject his voice, salvation and rule face judgment.

But people who trust and obey him are blessed.

He guides them along safe and peaceful paths until he brings them into the land of perfect light, purity and joy.

Moses also warned against false prophets.

We urgently need a reliable test for every message we hear, so that we can distinguish what God has spoken from what he has not.

Anything contradicting the clear meaning of the written word, or encouraging people to sin, cannot be a message from the Lord.

Cities of refuge and the distinction between murder and accident (verses 1–13)

The law distinguished between the blood of an innocent person who had been murdered and the guilt of the murderer.

It also provided cities of refuge so that a person would not die as a criminal for causing a death that was not intentional.

Jesus Christ, the Lord our Righteousness, is a refuge for sinners who flee to him through faith.

But there is no shelter in Christ for people who presume upon mercy while deliberately continuing in sin.

Those who flee from their sins to Christ are safe with him.

Those who expect him to protect them while they remain in their sins are deceiving themselves.

Boundary markers must not be moved (verse 14)

The Lord commanded Israel to preserve boundary markers in Canaan.

He wants everyone to know what belongs to them, and safeguards to be maintained so that no one wrongs another person or is wronged.

This is a moral command that continues to apply.

Each person should be content with their own portion and act justly toward neighbors in every matter.

False witnesses and public justice (verses 15–21)

A person must not be condemned on the word of only one witness.

Someone who deliberately gives false testimony should be subject to the penalty that the witness had attempted to inflict upon the accused.

Henry regards this as a just provision.

Christians should therefore be careful not only when giving evidence before a court but also in private conversation.

They must not join in slander.

And anyone whose conscience accuses them of sin should flee immediately to the refuge offered in Jesus Christ.

Israel's soldiers must trust God (verses 1–9)

In wars fought according to God's command, Israel could rely on his help.

The Lord, not the people's weapons or numbers, was to be their confidence.

In this respect their battles pictured the Christian's spiritual warfare.

Men unwilling to fight were to be released from the military campaign.

Sometimes their reluctance arose from family or other personal circumstances.

God did not want his service performed by people dragged into it against their will.

“Your people will offer themselves willingly” (Psalm 110:3).

Those who run the Christian race and fight the good fight of faith must set aside everything that makes them reluctant to do their duty.

People who were weak or afraid could also return home.

One reason was to prevent their fear from spreading to their fellow soldiers.

We must not adopt the fears of people who are afraid (Isaiah 8:12).

Peace offered and the limits of ancient warfare (verses 10–20)

Israel received laws about warfare against other nations.

Henry finds in the offer of peace a picture of God's gracious way of dealing with sinners.

He proclaims peace and urges them to be reconciled to him.

This also teaches us how to treat other people.

Even if others want war, we should want peace.

The ancient law included a different provision concerning towns within the territory promised to Israel, where idol worshipers were not to remain and lead the people astray.

Henry emphasizes an essential distinction: these regulations do not govern Christians' conduct today.

Christ's law of love, not Israel's ancient rules for conquest, is our rule.

The horrors of war bring anguish to a compassionate heart whenever we remember them.

They demonstrate humanity's wickedness, Satan's power and God's just judgment on a sinful world.

More dreadful still is the condition of those fighting against their own Maker, refusing even the fitting service of praise and worship.

Their destruction is certain.

Christians need not fear the number or power of their spiritual enemies, or their own weakness.

The Lord saves his people.

But anyone whose heart still clings to this world or fears Christ's cross and the conflict should not imagine the spiritual battle can be fought halfheartedly.

Even during a siege, Israel was forbidden to destroy fruit trees unnecessarily.

God cares for human welfare better than we care for it ourselves.

His commands protect our necessities and comforts, while uncontrolled appetite and passion destroy them.

Jewish interpreters understand this law to forbid deliberate waste of any kind.

Every creature of God is good.

We should not refuse his gifts, but we should never abuse them.

The things we carelessly destroy today may be exactly what we need tomorrow.

Verses 1-9
In the wars wherein Israel engaged according to the will of God, they might expect the Divine assistance. The Lord was to be their only confidence. In these respects they were types of the Christian's warfare. Those unwilling to fight, must be sent away. The unwillingness might arise from a man's outward condition. God would not be served by men forced against their will. Thy people shall be willing, [Ps.110.3] Psa 110:3. In running the Christian race, and fighting the good fight of faith, we must lay aside all that would make us unwilling. If a man's unwillingness rose from weakness and fear, he had leave to return from the war. The reason here given is, lest his brethren's heart fail as well as his heart. We must take heed that we fear not with the fear of them that are afraid, [Isa.8.12] Is 8:12.
[Deut.20.10-Deut.20.12]
Verses 10-12
The Israelites are here directed about the nations on whom they made war. Let this show God's grace in dealing with sinners. He proclaims peace, and beseeches them to be reconciled. Let it also show us our duty in dealing with our brethren. Whoever are for war, we must be for peace. Of the cities given to Israel, none of their inhabitants must be left. Since it could not be expected that they should be cured of their idolatry, they would hurt Israel. These regulations are not the rules of our conduct, but Christ's law of love. The horrors of war must fill the feeling heart with anguish upon every recollection; and are proofs of the wickedness of man, the power of Satan, and the just vengeance of God, who thus scourges a guilty world. But how dreadful their case who are engaged in unequal conflict with their Maker, who will not submit to render him the easy tribute of worship and praise! Certain ruin awaits them. Let neither the number nor the power of the enemies of our souls dismay us; nor let even our own weakness cause us to tremble or to faint. The Lord will save us; but in this war let none engage whose hearts are fond of the world, or afraid of the cross and the conflict. Care is here taken that in besieging cities the fruit-trees should not be destroyed. God is a better friend to man than he is to himself; and God's law consults our interests and comforts; while our own appetites and passions, which we indulge, are enemies to our welfare. Many of the Divine precepts restrain us from destroying that which is for our life and food. The Jews understand this as forbidding all wilful waste upon any account whatsoever. Every creature of God is good; as nothing is to be refused, so nothing is to be abused. We may live to want what we carelessly waste.
